## BENQODHI {.title-slide}

<div class="eyebrow">JRC Ispra · 10-11 September 2026</div>

<div class="title-word">BENQODHI</div>

<div class="subtitle">
BENchmarking Quantum Optimization:<br>
from Datasets to Health Innovation
</div>

<div class="lead">
A workshop to define credible shared benchmarks for quantum, AI, hybrid and
classical approaches in health and the life sciences.
</div>

::: {.notes}
Welcome everyone.

Start from the name BENQODHI and from the Boccaccio sentence. The exact sentence
still needs to be inserted by you. The point is to give a human opening: we are
not only here for a sequence of talks, but to put different communities in contact
and build something shared.

Then move quickly to the practical aim: benchmarks for quantum optimization, from
datasets to health innovation.
:::

## Why Now {.briefing-slide}

<div class="section-title">A moment of contact between fields</div>

<div class="briefing">
  <p><strong>AI is already changing scientific work.</strong> It changes how we
  model, search, explain, summarize and build tools.</p>

  <p><strong>Quantum computing may change what comes next.</strong> The practical
  impact is still emerging, but the strategic question is already real.</p>

  <p><strong>The interesting space is the exchange.</strong> AI for quantum,
  quantum for AI, and both tested against strong classical and hybrid methods.</p>
</div>

::: {.notes}
AI has already changed the scientific landscape and the way many of us work.

Quantum computing is not yet at the same practical stage, but a possible quantum
revolution is foreseen and is already shaping research, infrastructure and policy
decisions.

The opportunity is not AI versus quantum. The opportunity is the exchange between
fields, and the need for credible ways to compare progress.
:::

## Why Benchmarks {.briefing-slide}

<div class="section-title">Optimization is central, but the scope is wider</div>

<div class="briefing two-column">
  <div>
    <p><strong>Optimization</strong> is one of the main proposed application areas
    for quantum computing.</p>

    <p>But benchmarkable problems can also include <strong>sampling, inference,
    simulation, reconstruction</strong> and <strong>learning</strong>.</p>
  </div>

  <div>
    <p><strong>Shared benchmarks turn claims into comparable evidence.</strong></p>

    <p>They make it easier to compare methods, track progress, expose assumptions
    and decide where new approaches are genuinely useful.</p>
  </div>
</div>

::: {.notes}
One of the main possible applications of quantum computing is optimization, but we
should not make the workshop narrower than the science requires.

For health and biology, the relevant objects may also be sampling, inference,
simulation, reconstruction or learning, provided that they can be made into clear
benchmark tasks.

The reason benchmarks matter is simple: without common problems, metrics, baselines
and resource accounting, strong claims remain hard to compare.
:::

## Two Complementary Directions {.briefing-slide}

<div class="section-title">Controlled problems and real problems</div>

<div class="comparison">
  <div>
    <h3>Controlled problems</h3>
    <p>Theoretical, clean and repeatable.</p>
    <p>Close enough to real difficulty to be useful, but structured enough to
    measure performance of new AI, quantum and hybrid methods.</p>
    <p>Widely used in the literature, but still missing a systematic shared
    repository.</p>
  </div>

  <div>
    <h3>Health and biology problems</h3>
    <p>Genomics, imaging, mechanistic biology, clinical decisions and operational
    optimization.</p>
    <p>Messier, but scientifically meaningful.</p>
    <p>Inspired by the decathlon idea: a portfolio of challenges, not one problem
    pretending to represent everything.</p>
  </div>
</div>

::: {.notes}
We thought about two complementary approaches.

On one hand, controlled theoretical problems: these let us measure performance
carefully, and can connect to real computational difficulty. They are heavily used
in the literature, but not collected in a systematic way.

On the other hand, we want to build from health and biology. This requires looking
across different domains and extracting problems that are scientifically meaningful
and technically benchmarkable.

Daniel Egger's decathlon idea is a useful inspiration: not one benchmark, but a
portfolio where different challenges test different capabilities.
:::

## What This Workshop Should Produce {.briefing-slide}

<div class="section-title">From talks to shared outputs</div>

<div class="output-list">
  <p><strong>Today:</strong> talks as input from quantum, AI, optimization,
  biology, health, HPC and policy.</p>

  <p><strong>Tomorrow:</strong> five round tables on candidate benchmark problems,
  repository structure, community mechanisms and policy instruments.</p>

  <p><strong>Method:</strong> human expert discussion, supported where useful by
  AI-assisted note taking and document preparation.</p>

  <p><strong>Outputs:</strong> candidate problems, datasets or generators, metrics,
  baselines, resource accounting, repository structure, and possible paper, report,
  roadmap or policy note.</p>
</div>

<div class="closing-line">
Better benchmarks can improve comparability, collaboration, R&amp;D direction and
future public investment decisions.
</div>

::: {.notes}
The challenge is transdisciplinary. This is why the people in the room come from
different backgrounds: quantum algorithms, AI, optimization, statistical physics,
genomics, imaging, mechanistic biology, clinical optimization, HPC infrastructure
and policy.

The talks today are input. Tomorrow the workshop becomes more experimental: five
round tables, prepared themes, JRC note takers and facilitators, and AI-assisted
tools such as Kiro when they are useful.

The final aim is not just to collect presentations, but to leave with candidate
benchmark problems and a shared direction for the repository and possible follow-up
outputs.
:::
